summary: Describes the protocol elements, semantics and encodings of LDAP, which gives access to distributed directory services following X.500 models. The elements are based on the X.500 Directory Access Protocol. It is a proposed standard.

plainLanguage.summary: The language a computer uses to ask a big address book questions, like find this person, and to add or change entries.

subtitle: The wire protocol clients use to search, read and change entries in a networked directory.

tldr.problem: Programs need a standard way to look up and update entries in a distributed directory that follows the X.500 data and service models, without the weight of the full X.500 Directory Access Protocol.
tldr.mechanism: LDAP wraps every request and response in a common LDAPMessage envelope, defines a small set of operations (Bind, Search, Modify, Add, Delete, Modify DN, Compare, Abandon, Extended), and encodes them with a restricted form of ASN.1 BER over a reliable connection such as TCP.
tldr.outcome: RFC 4511 is the core protocol specification of LDAP version 3. It obsoletes RFC 2251, RFC 2830 and RFC 3771 and is a Proposed Standard.

today: RFC 4511 is a Proposed Standard and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It replaces RFC 2251, RFC 2830 (in part) and RFC 3771.

sections.title: What LDAP Is and How It Is Organised
sections.content:
The Directory is described as a collection of open systems cooperating to provide directory services. A directory user, which may be a person or another program, reaches it through a client, and the client talks to one or more servers using a directory access protocol. RFC 4511 details the protocol elements of the Lightweight Directory Access Protocol (LDAP), their semantics, and then how they are encoded and transferred.

The model is simple. A client sends a request describing an operation, and the server performs it in the Directory and normally returns a response. Operations are generally independent of each other, and each one is processed as an atomic action that leaves the directory in a consistent state. Nothing forces synchronous behaviour: requests and responses for several operations may be exchanged in any order.

The core operations map onto a subset of the X.500 Directory Abstract Service, but not one to one. A gateway to an X.500 directory may need several DAP requests to serve a single LDAP request.

This document is part of the LDAP Technical Specification and replaces earlier documents. It obsoletes RFC 2251 and RFC 3771 in their entirety, and obsoletes Sections 2 and 4 of RFC 2830.
sections.plainLanguage: Think of a huge phone book kept on a faraway computer. LDAP is the polite way of asking that computer to look something up or change a page, and the computer answers back.

sections.title: The Message Envelope and Common Elements
sections.content:
Every operation travels inside one envelope, the LDAPMessage. It holds a messageID, one protocolOp choice (a request or a response) and optional controls. The protocol is written in ASN.1 and sent using a subset of the Basic Encoding Rules.

The message ID ties responses to requests. A request MUST use a non-zero ID that differs from every other request in progress in the session, and typical clients just increment a counter. The value zero is reserved for unsolicited notifications from the server. The ID is an integer up to maxInt, which is 2147483647.

Strings are UTF-8 encoded characters in an LDAPString. Names of entries are distinguished names, and attribute values are opaque octet strings whose syntax is defined elsewhere. The RFC notes that there is no defined limit on a value's size, so values may be multi-megabyte, such as photographs. An implementation MUST NOT display or decode a value whose syntax it does not know.

Every response carries an LDAPResult with a resultCode, a matchedDN, a human-readable diagnosticMessage and an optional referral. Examples of result codes are success (0), noSuchObject (32) and invalidCredentials (49). If a server finds several errors it returns only one result code, the one that best indicates the nature of the error. Clients MUST NOT rely on the diagnostic text, because it is not standardised.

If a server cannot even recognise the message structure, it SHOULD send a Notice of Disconnection with protocolError and MUST end the session.
sections.plainLanguage: Every question and answer goes into the same kind of envelope with a number on it, so the sender can match each answer to the question it belongs to.

sections.title: Bind and Unbind: Starting and Ending a Session
sections.content:
The Bind operation exchanges authentication information and is best thought of as the authenticate operation. The request carries a version, a name and an authentication choice, either simple (a password) or sasl (a SASL mechanism name plus optional credentials). This document describes version 3. There is no version negotiation: the client sets the version it wants, and a server that does not support it MUST answer with protocolError. A server that does not support the chosen authentication choice returns authMethodNotSupported.

After sending a Bind, a client MUST NOT send further LDAP PDUs until it receives the BindResponse. Some SASL mechanisms need several round trips, and the client MUST NOT invoke other operations between the steps. A client may send further Binds later to change its authentication, and authentication from earlier binds is then ignored. Before a Bind is processed, all uncompleted operations MUST finish or be abandoned.

Text passwords sent with the simple choice are UTF-8, and clients SHOULD prepare them with the SASLprep profile first.

The Unbind operation is the quit operation. It is not the opposite of Bind, despite the name, which the RFC calls historical. After an Unbind request is sent and received, both sides gracefully end the session.
sections.plainLanguage: Bind is like showing your library card at the desk before you can borrow anything. Unbind is simply saying goodbye and leaving.

sections.title: The Search Operation
sections.content:
Search returns the entries that match a criterion, subject to access controls. The request names a baseObject to start from and a scope: baseObject (just that entry), singleLevel (its immediate children) or wholeSubtree (the entry and everything below it). A derefAliases setting controls whether alias entries are followed, and servers MUST detect looping while doing so.

The request also carries a sizeLimit and a timeLimit in seconds, where zero means no client-requested limit, and servers may enforce their own maximums. The typesOnly flag asks for attribute names without values. The attributes list chooses what to return: an empty list means all user attributes, an asterisk adds all user attributes to the named ones, and the special name 1.1 means no attributes at all. Operational attributes are only returned when listed by name.

The filter is built from and, or and not around tests such as equality, substrings, greater-or-equal, less-or-equal, presence, approximate match and extensible match. Filters use three-valued logic: TRUE, FALSE or Undefined. An entry is returned only when the filter is TRUE. A test on an attribute the server does not recognise is Undefined and not an error, so a filter on an unknown attribute such as shoeSize simply matches nothing.

Results come back as zero or more SearchResultEntry and SearchResultReference messages in any order, followed by exactly one SearchResultDone. A reference tells the client that part of the tree is held by another server, and the client must issue a new Search for each one. Clients that follow references MUST avoid loops and MUST be able to handle at least ten nested referrals.
sections.plainLanguage: Search is like asking a librarian to find every book on a shelf that matches your description. You say where to start looking, how deep to look, and what the book must be like, and you get a pile back.

sections.title: Changing and Comparing Entries
sections.content:
Several operations change the directory. Modify carries a list of changes, each one an add, delete or replace of an attribute's values. The whole list MUST be applied in order as a single atomic operation, so if the response reports an error the client may assume none of it was applied. The resulting entry must still satisfy the schema. Modify cannot remove the values that form the entry's name. That returns notAllowedOnRDN.

Add creates an entry. The entry MUST NOT already exist and its parent MUST exist. If the parent is missing, the server returns noSuchObject with the closest existing ancestor in matchedDN. Clients MUST NOT supply operational attributes that the server maintains itself, such as createTimestamp.

Delete removes one entry, and only leaf entries with no children can be deleted.

Modify DN renames an entry and can also move it under a new parent. The deleteoldrdn flag says whether the old name's values are removed. Clients MUST NOT expect to move entries freely between servers or naming contexts.

Compare asks whether an attribute holds a given value and answers compareTrue or compareFalse. This can be allowed even for attributes, like a password, that cannot be read directly.

Abandon asks the server to stop an earlier operation. It has no response, so the client cannot tell whether it worked. Abandon, Bind, Unbind and StartTLS cannot themselves be abandoned.
sections.plainLanguage: Changing the phone book is done carefully. A group of edits happens all together or not at all, you cannot rip out the line that is someone's name, and you can only tear out a page that has nothing attached to it.

sections.title: Controls, Extended Operations and Intermediate Responses
sections.content:
LDAP is built to grow without changing the base protocol. Controls attach extra semantics to an existing request. Each has an OID in controlType, a criticality flag and an optional value. If the flag is TRUE and the server cannot honour the control, it MUST refuse the operation with unavailableCriticalExtension. If the flag is FALSE, the server MUST ignore a control it does not support. This document itself defines no controls.

The Extended operation lets new request and response pairs be defined, identified by an OID in requestName. Servers list the controls and extensions they support as attributes of the root DSE. A request whose name is not recognised gets protocolError.

The IntermediateResponse message allows a single request to produce several responses. It SHALL NOT be sent unless the client's request, through an Extended operation or a control, specifically asks for it.

The same extensibility applies to the ASN.1 itself. Because sequences, sets, choices and enumerations are extensible, clients and servers MUST ignore trailing SEQUENCE components they do not recognise. Changes outside those mechanisms need a new protocol version.
sections.plainLanguage: It is like a phone book with blank slots for new features. You can staple on a note saying please do this too, and if the note is marked very important, a clerk who does not understand it must say no instead of ignoring it.

sections.title: Encoding, TLS and the Transport
sections.content:
LDAP expects a connection-oriented, reliable transport that delivers a stream of octets. The RFC illustrates the layers in a session: the transport connection at the bottom, an optional TLS layer above it, an optional SASL layer above that, and the LDAP message layer on top.

Messages use the Basic Encoding Rules with restrictions that ease encoding: only the definite length form, only the primitive form for octet strings, a BOOLEAN true is the byte FF, and a value equal to its default is left out.

Over TCP the encoded messages map straight onto the byte stream. Servers are recommended to listen on the IANA-assigned LDAP port, 389, though they may use another port, and clients MUST be able to contact servers on any valid TCP port.

The StartTLS operation, an Extended operation with OID 1.3.6.1.4.1.1466.20037, upgrades a session to TLS. The client MUST NOT send other LDAP PDUs until the response arrives and, if successful, TLS negotiation finishes. A server that does not support TLS returns protocolError. Either side may later remove the TLS layer with a closure alert.

A session ends normally when the client sends Unbind or the server sends a Notice of Disconnection (OID 1.3.6.1.4.1.1466.20036). Either side may abruptly close the connection if continuing would be pernicious. When the connection closes, a client MUST NOT assume that uncompleted updates succeeded or failed.
sections.plainLanguage: LDAP messages ride inside a reliable tube between two computers. Wrapping the tube in a locked pipe, which is what TLS does, keeps nosy people from reading what goes through.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
LDAP offers simple authentication with a cleartext password and any SASL mechanism, and SASL or TLS layers can add integrity and other protections. Cleartext passwords are strongly discouraged where the transport cannot guarantee confidentiality, and servers are encouraged to block directory modifications by anonymous clients.

SASL exchanges do not protect the version and name fields of a BindRequest or several fields of the BindResponse, so their contents SHOULD NOT be relied on unless protected another way, for example at the transport layer.

Security factors can change mid-session, for instance when credentials expire or a security layer is removed. Implementations should be robust about this and, for example, avoid returning sensitive data once confidentiality protection has gone. Caches that hold directory results MUST preserve access controls.

Referrals can be forged by a rogue application to push a client to a rogue server, so clients should consider rejecting referrals when confidentiality is not in place, and should reject referrals from StartTLS. Fields such as matchedDN, diagnosticMessage and codes like entryAlreadyExists can leak whether data exists, so servers should protect them as they protect the data. Peers MUST be ready for invalid and arbitrary-length encodings, and may abruptly close the session if they sense an attack.
sections.plainLanguage: Do not shout your password across a crowded room. Use a private channel, and be suspicious if a stranger says go ask someone else, because it might be a trick.
